newsitem.title: FRANCE: New French TV battle provides spicy summer saga.
newsitem.headline: New French TV battle provides spicy summer saga.

text.p: Battle has just broken out again between France's two warring television titans, private station TF1 and pay TV group Canal Plus, supplying thin summer news journals with a spicy saga.
On Monday Canal Plus said it asked the Paris commercial court to force France's terrestrial television channels to carry adverts for Canal Plus which they had refused last April.

Newspapers also reported on Monday that Television par Satellite (TPS), the digital satellite service operated by TF1, took Canal Plus to the competition court, alleging Canal Plus obstructed TPS from obtaining film rights. TPS and Canal Plus declined comment.

The outbreak is the latest of several skirmishes, in the courts and newspaper and magazine pages, which date from late last year when TPS was launched as TF1's head-on challenge to Canal Plus's monopoly in the French pay television, industry observers say.

The bitter rivalry has its roots in a personality clash between TF1 chairman Patrick Le Lay, a conformist and lover of classical music from a moneyed Breton Catholic family, and Canal Plus chairman Pierre Lescure, a non-conformist, rock music fan from a modest Communist family in the Paris suburbs, fortnightly news magazine Le Nouvel Economiste said in its latest issue.
The magazine devoted six pages to a character analysis of the two men who, it said, have had a relationship bedevilled by misunderstandings since 1986.

France is the only European country with four pay television services fighting for market share, Monday's issue of afternoon newspaper Le Monde said in an article devoted to competition between TPS and Canalsatellite, Canal Plus's satellite service.
"Everywhere else on the Old Continent, a single digital service takes on the job of collecting subscribers," Le Monde said.

"The main beneficiary of this battle of the titans is the consumer -- besides the noticeable increase in programme offerings, tariffs, following the example of TPS, are clearly falling," the newspaper said.
The French pay-TV market was pioneered by Canal Plus, which launched in 1984 and today has over 4.2 million subscribers.
Its Canalsatellite satellite TV service went digital in April 1996, while TPS launched in December 1996 and their smaller competitor, AB Productions' ABSat, launched in January 1997.

Canal Plus aims to have 4.3 million subscribers by the end of this year, Canalsatellite forecasts 500,000 digital subscribers by then, while TPS is seeking 300,000 and ABSat 75,000 subscribers by the year-end.
TPS seriously dented Canalsatellite's advance in the first four months of this year, Le Monde said, citing TV dealers.
An aggressive advertising campaign boosted TPS subscriptions, but delays in delivering its decoders fed back to clients who began to favour Canalsatellite in April and May, the newspaper said.
TPS has since then ended the problem with supply of its decoders, while Canalsatellite has adopted TPS's marketing approach, with agressive advertising and simple, low tariffs.
The two have also continued their war by treading on ground the other regards as its own preserve.

Canal Plus in June said it would launch a continuous news channel. Coincidentally such a channel would compete head-on with La Chaine Info (LCI), TF1's continuous news channel carried on cable networks and TPS.

TPS and TF1 both recently made inroads into acquiring film rights and concluding accords with independent French producers for co-productions, a domaine where Canal Plus, a specialist in cinema, has held sway.
Le Lay and Lescure, who personify France's television wars, each regard the other as an upstart, the magazine said.
Le Lay's career was at building firm Bouygues, which bought TF1 when it was privatised in 1987 and propelled Le Lay into the station's top slot.
Lescure, a journalist by training, made his name by launching rock music programmes on radio and television.
Their original mistrust has become outright hostility, the Nouvel Economiste said. "Nowadays, if you arrange a meeting with Le Lay, you do not invite Lescure," it said.
Canal Plus and TF1 originally planned to cooperate in digital satellite television, but talks which began in early 1994 ended in disarray over money, the magazine said.
"The (TF1) digital adventure was to happen without Canal. It would be against Canal. It was war," the magazine said.
